newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian funds target savings under the mattress.
newsitem.headline: Russian funds target savings under the mattress.

text.p: Russia's first unit investment fund was launched this week in a bid to tap the estimated $20 billion which wary savers have stashed under their mattresses.
The Pioneer First Fund went live on Tuesday, one of three funds so far approved by The Federal Commission for the Capital Markets securities watchdog.
All three funds should be launched by the end of the year. More than a dozen management companies have been licensed, a commission official said.
Fund managers acknowledge they are in uncharted territory but say the effect on the economy could be enormous.

"If it works well, it could dwarf the importance that the GKO (Treasury bill) market had for the development of the capital market," said Timothy Frost, director of the Pioneer Group's financial services activities in Russia.
Pioneer First is managed by KUIF, part of the First Voucher Fund (Pervy Vaucherny Fond in Russian), in which Pioneer acquired a 51 percent stake last year.

The government is eager to mobilise Russian private savings for investment in the cash-strapped economy and officials have estimated unit investment funds could attract up to 10 percent of the total. Unit investment funds (PIFs in Russian) are similar to British unit trusts.

But managers say there is much to do to win the confidence of Russian investors, many of whom had their fingers burnt in unlicensed, get-rich-quick funds which turned out to be no more than unsustainable pyramid schemes.
The most notorious was the MMM fund, which promised investors 3,000-percent dividends. Some made huge profits but many lost their life savings when MMM collapsed in 1994.

"There is just no trust among investors and it is going to be real hard work to persuade Russians that this is a vehicle they can have trust in and not just a pyramid scheme," said Beth Hebert, general director of Pallada Asset Management, which is set to launch the Pallada GKO fund on November 19.
The funds have retail investors in mind, with minimum investments of between 500,000 roubles ($91) and $500.

"People do not know where to invest their money. A lot of people who make decent money will tell you that," said Charles Mallory, chief executive of Credis (Moscow). Credis is part of the Credit Suisse group, which plans to offer shares in The Credis Fund for Short-Term Rouble Investment.
He said the biggest problem in the wake of the MMM scandal stemmed from misconceptions in the minds of investors whose first question was what return a fund could guarantee.
"The real problem is managing their expectations," he said.
The first funds will all invest in money market instruments, primarily the highly liquid and high-yield T-bills.
"These GKO and government paper fund are required in the initial stage to restore public confidence," Mallory said.
Frost said investing in T-bills made net asset values easier to calculate, settlement was easier and was tax exempt.
Russian authorities are keen to cut yields on T-bills to avoid crowding out investment to industry.
But fund managers say equity funds, or even direct investment funds, are further down the road.
"One of the things our market research showed was a clear distaste among retail investors for equities, particularly small-cap companies," said Mallory.
He said this was a legacy of the early days of privatisation when voucher funds, which invested privatisation certificates handed out to the public, went into small illiquid stocks.

Frost said unit investment funds would probably take off slowly. "It will not happen overnight and I hope it doesn't. It coudl happen over a number of months or a year. People have to be realistic and take a long view." ($1=5483 Rouble)
